name: Wei Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and the lead graphic designer for packaging at a small agency. I have a master’s degree in design and can turn a rough food label into a package the printer can actually cut and fold; the folding template and ingredient text have to fit together. I use our approved AI mockup tool now and then after another designer has tested a feature, but I check the actual dimensions and label copy myself. My salary is low for a lead designer, even though I handle the final client questions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much room do you have if the agency work changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a flat with my partner Imani, who teaches music lessons with hours that change by term, and we have no children. A repair to my bicycle left me with about three weeks of expenses saved, and there are few other design agencies nearby. My family respects a paid apprenticeship and a job done properly, but I cannot budget a promised lesson or lean on relatives for rent. A client should pay for a label that can be printed, not just a picture of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quick box mockup saves time in a meeting, but the printer still needs a folding template that closes. Last month a picture looked perfect until the legal ingredients wrapped onto the glue flap. I changed the type and measured the real carton again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the agency keeps most of its briefs in this mild version. My lead skill brings clients back, but three weeks saved is not enough to relax about a delayed invoice. Imani’s teaching income comes in patches, so I count the lessons she has actually been paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep designing paid food labels and checking the approved mockup against actual carton dimensions. Each payday, only if my full salary arrives and rent and groceries are covered, I would put fifteen into an emergency account. I would show the printer the corrected folding template before signing a client proof, as I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin cash buffer, although a faster mockup itself is welcome. A carton that will not close is a real cost to a small producer. Three weeks of savings would go quickly if my pay came late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put an unlaunched label into a public image service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not send a customer’s unlaunched ingredient list to a public generator. The approved tool can make the meeting picture, but the real carton template stays in our work system. I check it on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the fifteen come from if Imani has fewer lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifteen is new money from a full paid payday, not a label on what I already saved. If rent or food cannot be met, I skip that contribution. I will not ask Imani to assume extra lessons are booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the agency that AI can make thirty attractive label pictures before a client chooses a jar size. I would ask for paid testing of the new AI print-checker on old approved labels, not let it guess live ingredients. A good-looking preview cannot tell a food maker the glue flap swallowed the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ordinary mockup fees will fall, and my lead salary could be next if the owner prices only pictures. My packaging measurements and client trust still matter, but neither is a written full-week pay promise. Three weeks saved and few design vacancies make a shorter week a real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the agency permits it and pays the time, I would learn the new AI print-checker on twelve archived labels cleared for testing, comparing its warnings with the printer’s rejection notes. I would keep paid client layouts and ask the owner for written weekly design hours. If paid hours actually fall, I would compare posted paid prepress roles at local printers by written weekly wages and hours covering rent, utilities and bus fare; I would apply only if a shift bus runs and keep the agency job until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing part of my salary, though I would try a tested tool. I am willing to learn what other designers prove useful. I do not want a free evening of fixing bad labels to be called curiosity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test the new checker on a current unlaunched label?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use archived labels only if the agency cleared them for this test, with client names removed. If permission or paid time is missing, I would keep using the existing approved mockup and measure each carton myself. Live ingredient changes are too easy to mishandle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a printer role worth applying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A prepress opening would need a written complete week, not a day rate that looks high on a poster. I would check rent, utilities and bus fare against those wages and hours before applying. I would leave only after the offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Imani full AGI by 2028 could design the picture and fit the wording before a customer asks our agency for a quote. Robots folding cartons around 2031 are later; our design screens are exposed first. I would ask for actual paid project dates rather than reassurance about my master’s degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most paid label briefs could end, and three weeks saved would not bridge an unpaid search. Imani’s music lessons do not arrive as a fixed wage. There are only a few local design posts, and a printer may also bring in AI for prepress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would compare the last six payslips with rent, utilities and bus fare. If most paid agency hours end after 2028, I would apply for posted paid packaging-production work only where written weekly wages and hours cover those bills after travel, the first bus fits, and a supervisor confirms safe instruction on the cutting equipment. I would keep any paid agency hours until a suitable offer is signed; if no suitable opening appears after the hours end, Imani and I would ask the landlord about a schedule before rent is late, without assuming approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about an income gap that could eat three weeks of money almost at once. Knowing the folding template helps, but it does not mean I can operate a cutter safely. I would not turn a master’s degree into an excuse to skip instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you operate the cutting equipment immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not walk up to an unfamiliar cutter because I drew a package for one. I would ask who trains new production staff and see the safe process before accepting. That is a condition on doing physical work safely, not a claim that I already have the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the landlord already offered a payment schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have no landlord promise. We would ask only if most paid design hours actually ended without a suitable paid job, and we would bring our real figures before missing rent. I would not count my relatives as a fallback wage.

transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the agency five years is enough to learn what a printer will actually pay for: a label that passes the press, not another set of pictures. Thinking AGI could make layouts by 2031, with robots on carton lines around 2034. I would ask a printer about a real paid path before buying a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my folding-template skill may carry into prepress, but I cannot assume a higher salary just by changing desks. My three weeks saved cannot pay a course fee and rent at the same time. A proper apprenticeship would let me learn the press checks while earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would apply for a posted paid junior prepress opening only if the written weekly wages and hours cover rent, utilities and bus fare. If that opening requires the printer’s colour-control course, I would take it only after receiving the paid role, with the employer paying the course fee and my hours of attendance. I would keep paid agency projects until a suitable offer is signed; if the posting fails or my paid hours fall around 2031, I would look at other posted paid print shops by the same full-week test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about whether a printer will have a paid opening, but five years gives me time to ask what its work involves. A classroom alone will not keep the rent paid. I would prefer to learn beside a press operator while I still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the colour-control course before getting the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not buy the colour-control course before a role exists. It is only part of a posted paid opening that requires it, with the fee and paid attendance covered separately. If the printer offers only an unpaid placement, I would keep the agency wage and look elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the first printer has no paid opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether junior prepress staff actually check colour on the press or just copy AI labels into a queue. I would weigh that answer before accepting, but the hard test is still the written weekly wage and hours after fare and a signed offer. If no first opening appears, I would check other printers now rather than wait for 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona

I could learn more about the press if there is a paid opening, but I cannot budget a job that is not posted. A longer runway helps only if I put actual money aside now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I would keep my paid label work and save fifteen after each full salary payday once rent, groceries and utilities are covered. Every six months Imani and I would compare our actual wages, rent, travel and reserve. If design hours fall after 2036 and we still need my wage, I would apply for posted paid prepress only with written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after fare; I would leave only for a suitable signed offer and a bus that fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin cash buffer even with a decade on the card. A printer may have work, but I will not call it mine before it is advertised. A longer plan feels possible if the fifteen stays saved most paydays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a family date or count on relatives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not set a family date or ask relatives to bridge an unknown income gap. Imani and I would first need a reserve that survives rent and a surprise bill. Her next term of music lessons is not already paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the fifteen continue after shorter paid hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifteen is a new transfer only after a full payday and covered bills; I would skip it if salary hours fell. If we still need my wage after 2036, I would check the complete written week and the bus before leaving. I would not move because a printer used the word “creative” in a vacancy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because most packaging briefs might stop before a printer has a paid opening with a full week. Three weeks saved will not carry a long course or a search. Written agency dates and posted paid prepress work with clear weekly wages and hours would help Imani and me choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A picture of a box is easy to admire on a screen, but the actual carton has to close around a real product. I want to be paid for checking the actual carton fold before a client orders ten thousand.

headlineQuote: I want to be paid for checking the actual carton fold before a client orders ten thousand.
